# Modelling Classification


## Parametric Approach

A model with parameters $\theta$ outputs a score $\hat{y}^{(i)}$:

$$
\hat{y}^{(i)} = f(\theta, \vect{x}^{(i)})
$$

::: {.fragment}
$\theta$ — all learnable parameters (conv filters, FC weights, biases, …).
:::


## Softmax Classifier

Interpret outputs as **class probabilities**:

$$
P(Y = k \mid X = \vect{x}^{(i)}) = \sigma(\vect{z})_k = \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{j=1}^K e^{z_j}}
$$

::: {.fragment}
- $\vect{z}$ — **logits** (unbounded, real-valued)
- $\sigma(\vect{z})$ — valid probability distribution (sums to 1, all in $[0, 1]$)
:::


## Logits → Probabilities

```{python}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-classification-logits-to-probs
#| fig-cap: "Logits (left) → probabilities via softmax (right)."
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| out-width: 100%

from matplotlib import pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import seaborn as sns

np.random.seed(123)
logits = np.random.normal(size=(10,)) * 2
probs = np.exp(logits) / np.exp(logits).sum()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(ncols=2, figsize=(11, 4.5))

sns.barplot(x=list(range(10)), y=logits, ax=ax[0]).set(title="Logits")
sns.barplot(x=list(range(10)), y=probs, ax=ax[1]).set(title="Softmax", ylim=(0, 1))

ax[0].set_xlabel("Class")
ax[0].set_ylabel("Logit")
ax[1].set_xlabel("Class")
ax[1].set_ylabel("Probability")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.fragment}
Logits can be any real number — softmax always produces a valid distribution.
:::

## Cross-Entropy: The Idea

::: {.fragment}
A good model assigns **high probability to the correct class**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
- True class "deer", $P(\text{deer}) = 0.95$ → small loss
- True class "deer", $P(\text{deer}) = 0.02$ → very large loss (confidently wrong)
:::


## Cross-Entropy Formula

For one sample with one-hot label $\vect{y}$ and prediction $\hat{\vect{y}}$:

$$
CE = -\sum_{j=1}^K y_j \log \hat{y}_j
$$

::: {.fragment}
Since $\vect{y}$ is one-hot (only true class $c$ has $y_c = 1$):

$$
CE = -\log \hat{y}_c
$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
Just the **negative log-probability of the correct class**.
:::


## Cross-Entropy: Full Dataset

$$
L(\m{X}, \vect{y}, \theta) = -\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{j=1}^K y_j^{(i)} \log \hat{y}_j^{(i)}
$$

::: {.fragment}
Equivalent to **maximum likelihood** under the categorical model.
:::


## True vs. Predicted

```{python}
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-classification-cross-entropy
#| fig-cap: "True distribution (left) vs. predicted (right). CE measures the mismatch."

from matplotlib import pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import seaborn as sns

np.random.seed(123)
k = 5
logits = np.random.normal(size=(5,)) * 2
y_hat = np.exp(logits) / np.exp(logits).sum()
y_true = np.zeros_like(logits)
y_true[1] = 1

fig, ax = plt.subplots(ncols=2, figsize=(9, 3))
sns.barplot(x=list(range(k)), y=y_true, ax=ax[0]).set(title="True Distribution")
sns.barplot(x=list(range(k)), y=y_hat, ax=ax[1]).set(title="Predicted Distribution", ylim=(0, 1))
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```


## Asymmetric Penalty {.center}

::: {.incremental}
- **Confident & correct** ($\hat{y}_c \to 1$) → loss $\to 0$
- **Uncertain** ($\hat{y}_c = 0.5$) → loss $\approx 0.69$
- **Confident & wrong** ($\hat{y}_c \to 0$) → loss $\to \infty$
:::

::: {.fragment}
Drives models to be both **accurate** and **well-calibrated**.
:::


## Quiz: Which Loss is Higher?

A model predicts:

- $P(\text{deer}) = 0.4$ for an image that **is** a deer
- $P(\text{deer}) = 0.6$ for an image that is a **fox**

Which prediction gives the higher cross-entropy?

::: {.fragment}
**The first.** $-\log(0.4) \approx 0.92$ — low probability assigned to the true class.
:::

::: {.fragment}
For the second image, the true class is *fox* — only $P(\text{fox})$ matters, not $P(\text{deer})$.
:::


## Maximum Likelihood Connection

::: {.fragment}
Likelihood of the dataset:
$$
P(\vect{y} \mid \theta, \m{X}) = \prod_{i=1}^N \prod_{j=1}^K P(Y = j \mid X = \vect{x}^{(i)})^{y_j^{(i)}}
$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
Take $-\log$ → minimize → identical to cross-entropy.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Minimizing CE = maximizing likelihood.**
:::


# Architecture Overview


## The CNN Pipeline

::: {.fragment}
A CNN backbone extracts hierarchical features.
:::

::: {.fragment}
A classification head (e.g. an FC layer) maps features → $K$ logits.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Softmax + cross-entropy turn logits into a learnable classifier.
:::


## Architecture Progression {.center}

::: {.incremental}
- **AlexNet (2012)** — 8 layers, GPU-trained, won ImageNet
- **VGG (2014)** — 16–19 layers, all $3 \times 3$ kernels
- **ResNet (2015)** — 50–152+ layers via residual connections
- **ConvNeXt (2022)** — modernized CNN, competitive with Vision Transformers
:::


## AlexNet (2012)

::: {#fig-classification-alexnet2}
![@prince_understanding_2023]({{< meta params.images_path >}}alexnet_illustration.jpg){width=55%}

5 conv + 3 FC layers, 1000-way softmax. Trained on **two** GTX 580 GPUs (3 GB each).
:::

::: {.fragment}
The network had to be **split across GPUs** due to memory limits.
:::


## AlexNet — Loading via torchvision

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

import torch
import torchvision.models as models
import torchinfo

alexnet = models.alexnet()
x = torch.zeros(1, 3, 224, 224)
yhat = alexnet(x)

print(torchinfo.summary(alexnet, input_size=(1, 3, 224, 224)))
```


## VGG (2014)

::: {#fig-classification-vgg-arch}
![@prince_understanding_2023]({{< meta params.images_path >}}vgg_illustration.jpg){width=55%}

16–19 layers using only $3 \times 3$ kernels.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Design rule:** when spatial size halves, double the number of filters (preserves time complexity).
:::


## ResNet — The Problem

::: {#fig-classification-resnet-motivation1}
![Source: @He2016]({{< meta params.images_path >}}resnet_test_error.jpg){width=55%}

A 56-layer net is **worse** than a 20-layer net — on **train and test**.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Not overfitting — an **optimization problem**.
:::


## Residual Connections

::: {#fig-classification-residual-connection}
![Source: @johnson_eecs_2019]({{< meta params.images_path >}}residual_connection.jpg){width=55%}
:::

$$
\vect{x}_{l+1} = \vect{x}_l + F(\vect{x}_l)
$$

::: {.fragment}
Learn the **change**, not the full transformation.

If a layer has nothing to add: $F(\vect{x}_l) \approx 0$ → identity.
:::


## Why Residuals Work

::: {#fig-classification-skip-loss-landscape}
![Source: @li_visualizing_2018]({{< meta params.images_path >}}loss_landscape_skip.png){width=70%}

Loss landscape: without (left) vs. with (right) skip connections.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Skip connections **smooth the loss surface** → optimization works.
:::

## Which Architecture? {.center}

::: {.fragment .highlight-red}
**Don't be a hero.**
:::

::: {.fragment}
Use proven, off-the-shelf architectures:
:::

::: {.incremental}
- **ResNet-50 / ResNet-101** — reliable baseline (slightly dated)
- **EfficientNet** — when size or speed matters
- **ConvNeXt** — SOTA CNN, competitive with ViTs
:::

::: {.fragment}
Choose based on accuracy, FLOPs, memory, available data.
:::


# Summary {.center}


## Key Takeaways

::: {.incremental}
- Classification has variants — **multi-class, binary, multi-label, multi-task**
- **Softmax** turns logits into a valid probability distribution
- **Cross-entropy** = $-\log \hat{y}_c$ — punishes confident wrong predictions hard
- Architecture trend: **AlexNet → VGG → ResNet → ConvNeXt**
- **Residual connections** smooth the loss landscape, enable depth
- **Don't be a hero** — start with a proven backbone
:::
